description: We are a 6-member in-person student team taking on the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Our skills include software development, UI/UX, game logic, research, problem-solving, and presentation. We aim to build a fun, educational game that teaches young users how to manage resources and make decisions during a Moon or Mars mission. Our team is already complete and not seeking additional members.
summary: Welcome to Lost Signal! For NASA's Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer Challenge, Our Team set out to create more than a survival game: an interactive mission where every decision can shape the future of an entire crew. After a navigation failure forces their spacecraft into a harsh emergency landing on Mars, six astronauts must work together to survive and establish a habitable outpost. But Mars won't make it easy. As the player, you take command of the mission, managing power, water, food, construction, life support, and crew safety while facing environmental hazards such as dust storms and solar radiation alerts. There is no single correct way to build the colony. Every structure consumes resources, every operating system has a cost, and every decision creates new possibilities and risks. Inspired by NASA space-weather data, including DONKI, Lost Signal transforms the challenges of establishing a human presence beyond Earth into a story-driven, interactive adventure.
details:
Lost Signal's Project Solution

Lost Signal is an educational survival and colony-management game designed to introduce players to the challenges of establishing a sustainable human presence on Mars.

The game begins with an emergency landing caused by a navigation-system malfunction. With communications damaged, water recovery offline, and part of the solar power system unavailable, the crew must manage their remaining resources while restoring communications and reaching a previously supplied cargo site.

Once there, the real mission begins: transforming delivered equipment and construction modules into a functioning Martian outpost.

Unlike traditional mission-based games that force players through a fixed sequence of objectives, Lost Signal gives players freedom to choose their construction priorities and resource-management strategies. Multiple missions can progress in parallel, and each decision has consequences for the colony's power, water, food, equipment, and crew.

How Does Our Solution Work?

The game is divided into two chapters, taking the player from an emergency landing to the establishment of a Martian outpost.

Chapter 1 — The Emergency

The story begins when the spacecraft experiences a navigation-system failure. Inertial navigation readings disagree with the backup instruments, making automated precision landing unreliable. Commander Franklin takes manual control, resulting in a harsh but survivable landing.

After the landing, the crew discovers several problems:

  • Communications are offline.
  • One solar array has failed to deploy.
  • The water-recovery system is offline.
  • The emergency battery has an estimated 41 hours of endurance at the previous consumption rate.

The player takes control of the spacecraft's command station and learns how to manage the available resources.

Through interactive checkpoints, players must:

  • Switch off nonessential equipment to reduce power consumption.
  • Maintain safe cabin temperature and air quality.
  • Allocate electricity for communications diagnostics without compromising life support.
  • Manage stored water and electricity while repairs continue.

Once communications are restored, the crew sends an emergency report and their available navigation readings. Following the Earth–Mars communication delay, Mission Control confirms their estimated location and provides route-planning information. The crew then travels to the cargo site where equipment delivered by a previous expedition is waiting.

Chapter 2 — Building a Habitable Outpost

The second chapter is the main colony-management experience. It takes place across six simulated Martian sols, each divided into three phases: daylight, late daylight, and night.

The player must establish a functioning outpost while balancing several interconnected missions.

1. First Shelter

The crew needs a functioning habitat before they can establish a permanent presence on Mars.

Players must construct the habitat using the delivered modules and activate Life Support to provide air handling and heating. They must also prepare enough stored electricity to maintain essential systems through the first Martian night.

2. The First Harvest

Food production becomes a priority once the habitat is operational.

Players can construct a greenhouse and activate its growing systems. However, crops require electricity, water, and suitable growing conditions. Keeping the greenhouse operational supports food production but increases resource consumption.

Players must decide how much of their available resources they can afford to dedicate to agriculture.

3. Every Drop Counts

Water is another essential resource for the colony.

Players must maintain the drinking-water reserve above a required safety level for consecutive gameplay phases. They can conserve water, construct a water recycler, or manage other water-consuming services.

The recycling system helps recover water from collected wastewater, but it also requires electricity to operate.

4. The Dust Storm

The crew receives a dust forecast before a storm reaches the outpost on Sol 3.

During the storm, solar generation is reduced, making stored battery energy more important. Players must decide which services can continue operating without jeopardizing essential systems.

When the storm clears, dust remains on the solar arrays, reducing their efficiency. The crew automatically cleans one array at a time when conditions are safe, allowing the remaining arrays to continue generating electricity.

5. The Red Planet Experiment

Scientific exploration becomes another objective once the colony has established its basic infrastructure.

Players can choose between two approaches:

  • Field Survey: Send a crew member outside with scientific instruments to examine Martian rocks and ground conditions.
  • Lab Analysis: Construct a research bench and analyze a sample already available at the cargo site.

Both approaches can produce a valid scientific observation, but they have different resource requirements and operational risks.

6. Shield Against the Sun

A solar-particle alert is forecast on Sol 5 before the radiation event begins.

Players must consider crew locations, outdoor activities, and available protection. Astronauts conducting fieldwork or other outdoor assignments are more exposed than those inside protected areas.

The player must manage the crew's safety while maintaining essential outpost operations. The event also introduces the importance of protective infrastructure and radiation-aware mission planning.

7. The Message Home

Once a valid scientific observation has been collected, the crew can prepare to send its findings to Earth.

Players must construct and power the communications relay. Transmitting the report and receiving Earth's response are separate stages, requiring the communications system to be operational when needed.

The final objective evaluates the colony's progress, available resources, and ability to maintain essential systems.

Player Freedom and Resource Trade-offs

One of Lost Signal's main gameplay features is that players are not forced to follow one construction sequence.

The player can choose between building additional solar arrays to increase electricity generation or constructing battery banks to store more energy for nighttime and emergencies.

Similarly, players can prioritize greenhouse production, water recycling, research, or other infrastructure depending on their current resources and mission objectives.

The available outpost-management actions are:

  • Build: Construct a building, module, or infrastructure upgrade.
  • Turn On: Activate an available service.
  • Turn Off: Suspend an operating service to reduce resource consumption.

Missions describe objectives and challenges rather than prescribing which building the player must construct. Multiple objectives can progress simultaneously when resources, available crew, and environmental conditions allow it.

Every decision has a trade-off, and the consequences are calculated through the game's programmed resource-management and simulation rules.

Educational Value

Lost Signal aims to make the engineering and scientific challenges of space exploration understandable through gameplay.

Instead of presenting players with complicated scientific reports, the game places them in situations where they experience the importance of:

  • Power generation and energy storage.
  • Life-support systems and environmental control.
  • Water recovery and resource conservation.
  • Food production and greenhouse management.
  • Radiation protection and crew safety.
  • Scientific observation and communications.
  • Planning, prioritization, and decision-making under limited resources.

The game is designed to make these concepts accessible to younger audiences while retaining meaningful decisions inspired by real space-exploration challenges.
